chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Shu'ayb, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who came to a group of people and claimed a house that was in their possession, and the one in whose hand the house was established the proof that he had inherited it from his father, and it was not known how its matter was. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'The one with the most proof is made to swear an oath, and it is handed over to him.'

And he (peace be upon him) mentioned that a group of people came to Ali (peace be upon him) disputing over a mule. So the proof was established for these ones that they had bred it in their stable, and neither had they sold it nor had they gifted it; and those ones established the proof that they had bred it in their stable, and neither had they sold it nor gifted it. So he (peace be upon him) judged by it based upon the one with the most proof, and made them swear an oath.

He (the narrator) said, 'So I asked him (peace be upon him) at that time, 'What is your view if the one who claimed the house...?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If the father of the one who was in it acquired it without a price, and the one who was in it cannot establish proof except that he inherited it from his father?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'If its matter is like that, then it is for the one who claims it and establishes the proof for it.'
ai.seo_question: How does Islamic jurisprudence resolve property disputes when both parties present evidence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of 'Al-Aktharuhu Bayyinatan' (the one with the stronger proof) as a primary mechanism for resolving ownership disputes in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that the judge evaluates the quality and quantity of evidence rather than merely relying on possession. The narrative highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (AS) application of this rule by referencing Imam Ali’s (AS) judgment in a dispute over a mule, demonstrating the continuity of legal reasoning from the Ahl al-Bayt. It further clarifies that if the current possessor lacks a valid transfer deed and relies solely on inheritance without proof of acquisition, the claimant with superior evidence prevails, reinforcing the importance of documented proof in property law.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Al Husayn, from Safwan, from Shuayb, from Abu Baseer who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the man who came to a group of people and claimed for a house which was in their hands, and the one in whose hand was the house established the proof and he had inherited it from his father, and it is not known how was his matter’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The one with the most proof would have to swear an oath, and it would be handed over to him’.

And he<sup>asws</sup> mentioned that they came to Ali<sup>asws</sup> with a group of people disputing regarding a mule. So the proof was established for these ones that they had bred it in their stable, and neither had they sold it nor had they gifted it; and those ones established the proof that they had bred it in their stable, and neither had they sold it nor gifted it. So he<sup>asws</sup> judged by it based upon the one with the most proof, and made them swear an oath’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘So I asked him<sup>asws</sup> at that time, ‘What is your view that there was one who claimed for the house?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If the father of the one who was (living) in it acquired it without a price and the one who was in it cannot establish (proof) except that he had inherited it from his father?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If it was like that, so it is for the one who claims it and establishes the proof for it’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan from Shu’ayb from abu Basir who has narrated the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who comes to a certain people and claims the house. It is in their possession but he claims to be his house. The one who has the house in his possession presents testimony that he has inherited it from his father but does not know more about it. He (the Imam) said, The party that has the greater degree of testimony is asked to take an oath and it then is given to him.’

He (the Imam) then mentioned that once a certain people came before Ali, ‘Alayhi al-Salam. They had a dispute over a mule. There was testimony that this party had bred it in their barn, which they did not sell, or gift; and the other party presented testimony that they had bred it in their barn and had not sold or gifted. He (the Imam) issued a judgment in favor of the party with a greater degree of testimony and asked him to take an oath.

I then asked about the one who claims a house to be his house. He (the Imam) said, Tf the father of the one who lives there had taken it without price and the one living in it did not present testimony but that he has inherited it from his father’, he (the Imam) said, Tf this is the case it then belongs to the one who has claimed it and has presented testimony.’” (In al-Masalik it is said that when testimonies contradict and the asset is in their hand they each receive one-half)
